item.title: How Did Aging Muscles Trade Strength for Protection?
item.description: As we grow older, our muscles shift from fast-twitch to slow-twitch fibers — and scientists now believe this is not just a sign of decline, but a clever survival strategy that trades power for protection.

item.title: How Did Dunwoody College Students Build a Brand-New Car for a Minneapolis Veteran?
item.description: Dunwoody College of Technology automotive students refurbished a 2020 Hyundai Elantra for a US Navy veteran through the NABC Recycled Rides for Schools program, giving him the freedom to reach doctor's appointments and daily errands.

item.title: Can a Roll of Tape Really Beat Sandbags at Keeping Floodwater Out?
item.description: A UK experiment showed that ordinary rolls of tape can block up to 99% of floodwater sneaking past a door, easily beating the 70% kept out by traditional sandbags — a handy trick for families when a storm surge hits with little warning.

item.title: How Did Mayo Clinic Discover New Ways to Fight Zombie Cells That Drive Aging?
item.description: Scientists at Mayo Clinic have uncovered fresh details about 'zombie' cells — aging cells that linger in the body and fuel inflammation. Seven new studies map how these cells differ, why they harm us, and how everyday compounds like the one in tomatoes might help fight back.

item.title: How Did Jupiter Use an Invisible Shield of Plasma Waves to Deflect the Solar Wind?
item.description: Jupiter's Juno spacecraft discovered the gas giant's bow shock works like a cosmic symphony, using plasma waves with multiple frequencies to deflect the solar wind.

item.title: How Did Einstein's Equations Challenge the Need for Dark Energy?
item.description: For decades, scientists have assumed that a mysterious 'dark energy' is pushing the universe apart faster and faster. But new mathematical work from UC Davis suggests that Einstein's original equations might naturally produce cosmic acceleration on their own — without dark energy at all.

item.title: How Are Canada and the EU Planning an Ever-Closer Partnership at Their Montreal Summit?
item.description: At a summit in Montreal, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney laid out a bold vision for an 'associate membership' partnership — the EU's closest relationship with any country outside Europe.

item.title: Who Was Panther Pat, the First Woman to Play Pro Football?
item.description: In 1970, Pat Palinkas stepped onto a football field as the placekick holder for the Orlando Panthers — becoming the first woman to play professional football in a men's league. Fifty years later, a stop-motion documentary called \"Panther Pat\" brings her forgotten story back to life.

item.title: How Did a Simple Roll of Tape Beat Sandbags at Stopping Flood Water?
item.description: Tests at the University of Hull found that everyday synthetic tape can block up to 99% of flood water from sneaking through a doorway — far better than heavy, clumsy sandbags.

item.title: How Did Romans Make Color-Changing Glass 1,600 Years Ago — And Can Science Copy It Today?
item.description: A 4th-century Roman glass cup changes color from green to red depending on how you light it — and scientists just decoded the secret that might be the world's first nanotechnology.

item.title: What Amazing Secrets Has the Tower of London Kept for 1,000 Years?
item.description: For nearly a millennium the Tower of London has worn many crowns: royal palace, armoury, treasury, menagerie, mint, and prison. Its stones have witnessed daring rescues, disguises, a jewel heist, and the footsteps of kings, queens, and even a few famous beasts.

item.title: How Did a TikTok Video Reveal a Whole New Kind of Underground Fish?
item.description: A pale, translucent fish with skin-covered eyes was hiding in plain sight — spotted not on a research expedition, but in a TikTok video showing it emerging from a borewell in India.

item.title: How Did Scientists Date 128,000-Year-Old Ice From Tibet?
item.description: Ancient ice cores drilled from the Guliya Ice Cap in Tibet carry climate secrets stretching back more than 128,000 years — far older than scientists once believed. By studying radioactive isotopes, researchers built the first reliable timeline for these frozen archives.

item.title: How Do Tiny Plants Help Keep Microplastics Out of the Ocean?
item.description: A clever new invention mimics the way ultrahydrophobic plants in wetlands trap microplastic particles, and it is already pulling more than 98% of them out of wastewater flowing toward the Atlantic Ocean.

item.title: Do Spiders Dream? What Their Nightly Twitches Might Mean
item.description: Scientists have discovered that spiders experience two clear sleep stages — including a REM-like phase with eye movements and muscle twitches. Could our eight-legged roommates be having tiny spider dreams?

item.title: Could Coconut Oil Power the Next Generation of Jet Fuel?
item.description: Scientists in Japan have turned discarded coconut oil into a sustainable aviation fuel that runs in a real jet engine, cuts pollution, and uses waste that would otherwise go to landfill.

item.title: How Did a Texas Barber Return $128,000 He Found at an ATM to Its Owner?
item.description: A man in Lewisville, Texas spotted a bag stuffed with over $128,000 in cash and checks sitting beside a Bank of America ATM. Without a second thought, he called the police and helped make sure every single dollar got back to its rightful owner.

item.title: Less Than 42 Minutes of Bright Daylight Linked to Higher Dementia Risk
item.description: Getting sunlight — even on a cloudy day — may be one of the simplest ways to help protect your brain as you age. A large study following nearly 90,000 adults found that spending 42 minutes or more each day in bright daylight was associated with a 17 percent lower risk of dementia.

item.title: How Did a New Yorker Named Service Clean Up a Brooklyn Dumping Site All on His Own?
item.description: When Joshua Service spotted a filthy dumping site under a Brooklyn bridge, he didn't just call 311 — he grabbed gloves and cleaned it up himself, filling ten trash bags in two hours and inspiring his whole neighborhood.

item.title: How Did an Ancient Eclipse Show Earth Spun Faster 2,700 Years Ago?
item.description: A total solar eclipse witnessed by ancient Chinese astronomers in 709 BCE let researchers pin down how much faster Earth spun back then — and revealed that our star was waking up from a long quiet spell.
